name: Antagonists

covenants.name: The Cathedral of St. John the Apostle
covenants.notes:
Written up as a covenant, as The Church pp. 48-51 allows. The bishop may use its resources as a magus uses his covenant's (Ant p. 52). 502 Build Points. The Hooks and Boons are from The Church and Covenants.

Divine aura 5, rising to 6 in the Lady Chapel (p. 52).

Specialists (p. 52): provost of canons (Theology 5), chief chorister (Holy Music 8), 4 Cantores (Ceremony 5), 3 canons (Organization Lore: Church 5), archdeacon (Civil & Canon Law 7), 2 notaries (Profession: Scribe 5), exorcist (Divine Lore 6), deacon (Profession: Steward 5), 4 doorwardens (Brawl 5), 8 acolytes used as clerks, scribes, messengers and distributors of alms (Organization Lore: Church 4).

Setting it in a saga (p. 50): it fits most cities of western Mythic Europe. It need not be dedicated to St. John, but could still hold a major relic of his, since where the Hand lies is not known. Outside the Roman Church, change the details to suit Eastern Christianity.

possessions.name: The Hand of St. John the Apostle
possessions.description:
The hand that wrote the fourth Gospel, three Epistles and the Book of Revelation, and one of Christendom's most significant relics. St. John, the Beloved Disciple, guardian of the Blessed Virgin and brother of St. James the Greater, died at Ephesus. He and James were called the Sons of Thunder.

Faith score 4, so 4 Faith Points and a Divine Might of 40 (p. 52). It gives its bearer Magic Resistance 40 (p. 66).

Turn Back the Missile, 2 points, Init +5, appropriate Form: at Range Voice, guards up to 10 people from any missile, thrown, shot or moved by magic, and hurls each back at whoever sent it. The attacker defends against his own attack; any Penetration uses the relic's Might. It lasts until no longer needed, typically the end of the fight. It copies one of the saint's miracles.

Curse of Drowning, 2 points, Init +8, Aquam: the target vomits sea water and begins to drown, for as long as the wielder concentrates or chooses. The target can do nothing else and makes Deprivation rolls (ArM5 pp. 180-181) every 30 seconds. If the target lives, any wounds from drowning become Long Term Fatigue levels.

possessions.name: The Rib of St. Martin of Tours
possessions.description: A relic of the patron of beggars, horsemen and soldiers, a saint popular in France and Italy. Faith score 2, so 2 Faith Points and a Divine Might of 20. Its holder can activate the saintly power Grant of Serenity (RoP: The Divine Revised Edition p. 88).

possessions.name: A Fragment of the True Cross
Other minor relics
possessions.description: Three more minor relics, each of Faith score 1.

possessions.name: Tears of St. John
possessions.description: Tears on the statue of St. John.

possessions.name: Easter Echoes
possessions.description: Echoes in the cathedral following Easter Mass.

possessions.name: Chancel Water
possessions.description: Water washed off the chancel steps.

covenants.summary:
The seat of the diocese, in a city near the covenant. A relic of St. John the Apostle draws a steady stream of pilgrims, who are both a nuisance and an income to the cathedral's staff and congregation.

The bishop is served by a secretary, several archdeacons, a chapter of canons and a crowd of assistants in minor orders. Each archdeacon runs the canon court and the Church's interests in his own archdeaconry; the canons keep the cathedral and sing in the choir that has made it famous.
covenants.what_matters:
Hook: Pilgrimage Site (Major) (Surroundings); Urban (Major) (Site)
Boon: Aura (Major) (Site); Chapter of Canons (Minor) (Church); Edifice (Minor) (Lady Chapel, Fortifications); Edifice (Minor) (Chancel, Fortifications)

neighbours.name: Arques
neighbours.summary: A lordship in the Duchy of Normandy, and the birthplace of its baron. His family's fortune was made there when King John lost his French holdings and they stood with the winners.

neighbours.name: York Cathedral School
neighbours.summary: The cathedral school of York in the north of England, where Edwin Locke is a well-known tutor.

neighbours.name: The Barony of Arques
neighbours.summary:
A lesser barony of ten manors, owing the service of ten knights and a hundred infantry. Its lands lie partly round Arques in Normandy and partly in a few sizable manors near the covenant, where the baron has not lived long enough to learn the language.

At first his court looks like that of any rich noble, if with an eye for the unusual and a readiness to pay for the best.
neighbours.secrets: Every family tie is a lever: track the children's ages, because the baron's marriages for them and his fears for them can be used against him (Ant p. 10). As a wealthy lord he need give only a season a year to his estates, and in time he fails even that (Ant p. 17).

neighbours.name: Geoffroi's Council of Wizards
neighbours.summary: A gathering of scholars and practitioners of many traditions at the baron's court, kept at his expense. The baron compares it to the court of Sicily, where scholars of many cultures work side by side, and speaks of shared learning and peaceful understanding.

details.decides: The baron as patron, with the prominent and most socially tolerable members guiding him.
details.wants: Learning from strange traditions, safety at court, and as much as the baron will give.
details.offers: Counsel, curiosities, and works of magic and philosophy to the baron's order.

neighbours.secrets:
Most members are unGifted, because of what The Gift does to company; one or two with the Gentle Gift may lead. Since a tradition takes an opened Gift or a ritual Initiation, they exchange only knowledge of the realms, of the Order, and of each other's traditions (Ant p. 11).

Under the talk of learning, their shared concern is to get all they can from the baron. They counsel him and manage what he sees of the world, and give him trinkets for security and funds: at court each enjoys the effect of the Wealthy Virtue, an extra season of study (Ant p. 11).

Output (Ant p. 11): one average tractatus on Magic, Faerie or Infernal Lore for each practitioner; one or two inceptions and formulae a year; one enriched object a year; 10 levels of other enchantments a year. The collection may be studied book by book or as realia (Covenants p. 102; Ant p. 15).

Lesser folk touched by magic, not on the council (Ant p. 13): a mundane astrologer and philosopher, skilled in inceptions, who wants true magic; a blind beggar cursed with prophetic visions, who would trade one sight for the other; a young boy who sees ghosts, and the mother who took him from their frightened village; a faerie-touched armorer of great skill, who needs a place to work, money for his workshop, and someone to deal with the faerie forever trying to take back its tools.

Sample inceptions (Art & Academe ch. 5; the astrologer knows how to make each, and a season makes copies, finished by casting the horoscopes): Has N Betrayed the Confidence of NA?, level 5, Binary (Base 4, +1 past), whether the first person has probably revealed a secret of the second: Geoffroi uses it on Ysabeau. Is N the Father of NA?, level 5, Binary (Base 5), which reads the boy's present state, not the past: Geoffroi uses it on François (Ant p. 21).

Sample reagent: Glass of Uncommon Purity, level 20, Substantial (Base 10, +2 Substantial), purifies glass as it is worked; decanters and glasses of it give a host +2 to Leadership while entertaining guests (Ant pp. 21-22).

Sample theriacs: Compress of Tormentil, level 15, Mild (Base 10, +1 Mild), a bandage of tormentil and comfrey that heals a Light Wound from a slashing or piercing weapon in a week. Tincture of Vitality, level 15, Moderate (Base 5, +2 Moderate), a draft that at once lifts Tired to Weary: Geoffroi uses these at the tourney (Ant p. 22).

Without Art & Academe, use only the effects (Ant p. 21). The amulets, chartae and wondrous items are device records.

neighbours.name: Baron Geoffroi's Hunger for Magic
neighbours.summary: A rich and curious baron near the covenant starts to take an interest in magic, and in the scholars next door.

stages.title: First Encounter
stages.clues: One of these, the others free for later (Ant pp. 13-14). A magical stag of little might, fleeing his chase, is trapped against the Aegis with his hounds behind it. A demon that priests could not drive out jumps to a new host, and a grog may carry it into the covenant. A great egg-smooth stone wrecks a farmer's hayloft and no team of oxen can lift it. A strange leper, whom he drove off and who cursed him, is in truth a wandering Tytalus magus, and the baron's son lies deathly ill.
stages.ignored: He leaves curious, distrusting his Gifted helpers, and feeling there may be others more amenable.

stages.title: The Library
stages.clues: He tries to buy or commission books or hire a tutor, sure that a book of spells is all he needs, and asks to be sent on to other wizards if refused. A city merchant offers him texts that prove to be on Infernal Lore, and the covenant is asked to verify them. He visits a regio, and a week later Claude comes for help: the baron is at chess with a powerful faerie for his companions' lives (Ant pp. 14-15).
stages.ignored: He has the start of a collection of grimoires, bestiaries and strange objects.

stages.title: The Hunt
stages.clues: He asks for a magically keen pack of hounds, turning belligerent if he has seen a familiar. He invites the magi to capture a faerie-touched sounder of boar, offering first choice of the cuts; alone his party comes back bloodied and a man short. He offers a bounty for beasts of virtue brought alive, risking the covenant's allies and vis. A man who turns wolf at the full moon claims sanctuary from him, wanted as the quarry of a magical hunt (Ant p. 15).
stages.ignored: He is not yet dangerous, but has become a nuisance.

stages.title: The Tournament
stages.clues: Planned a year ahead for spring or summer. He commissions an enchanted sword, a golden cup of grandeur, a horse of virtue and a magical hawk, as well as magical entertainments for the feast, pays well, wants help for his own knights, and invites the covenant to enter. Where kings frown on tournaments, as in Stonehenge, he asks the magi to spy out how to win the king's favor, or goes to an astrologer (Ant pp. 15-16; Lords of Men p. 64).
stages.ignored: Helping him may bring rivals to other wizards, and more charges of interfering with mundanes.

stages.title: The Council of Wizards
stages.clues: He assembles his council and invites the magi to join and share their magic. One of the cunning folk (Hedge Magic Revised Edition p. 101) comes to the land and is held as a witch. The wizards seek Bonisagus' theory in exchange for insights, and ask what the magi will give instead of Parma. He promises Alenard to a magician, and Ysabeau pleads with the covenant. A Quaesitor comes to investigate the covenant's support for him, with old scores to settle (Ant pp. 16-17).
stages.ignored: The covenant gains the Rival External Relations Hook (Covenants p. 22).

stages.title: Stolen Resources
stages.clues: Vis sources are stripped, and the trail leads to a court wizard; Geoffroi offers to protect them all, if only he is told of them. The council claims every aura, beast of virtue and Gifted child on his lands just as a magus hears of a Gifted child. A nearby covenant, its own sources raided, holds the characters' covenant to blame and demands reparation (Ant p. 17).

stages.title: The Theft of Parma
stages.clues: A court wizard plots to abduct a magus or apprentice and force a season's teaching of Parma Magica. The council may not know. The troupe can play the abductors, planning around Aegis and Parma (Ant p. 17). The Gift is needed to use Parma, so most of them cannot, and a score of 1 is probably the least worth teaching.
stages.ignored: The Order would stop at nothing to prevent it, and retribution and debate over who is to blame would follow.
stages.stopped: Dealt with quickly and quietly, before word gets out.

stages.title: Fines and Taxes
stages.clues: Heavy tallage, tolls and fines to pay for it. Hardship sends the covenant to a far fair. Stolen crops lead to his new tax collector. Bandits capture a Redcap, and their leader's stolen devices make her look like one of his wizards (Ant p. 17).
stages.ignored: With Covenants' Wealth & Poverty rules, each type of inhabitant costs 1 point more (Covenants p. 63).

stages.title: A Poor Ruler
stages.clues: Ysabeau, banished for opposing Alenard's fate, passes the grogs an Arcane Connection to herself as she goes under guard to an outlying estate with her daughters. A rival lord's men search travellers. Agitators blame the covenant for leading the baron astray, perhaps as a distraction. Serfs flee to the covenant, and Claude comes with armed men, promising only the ringleaders will suffer (Ant p. 18).

stages.title: The Expulsion of Claude
stages.clues: Geoffroi dismisses his steward for one gifted in magic, perhaps Edwin Locke. Claude retires to a monastery in Normandy (Ant p. 18).
stages.turned: He has gathered Arcane Connections to the court's magicians, some still active, and might give them up if he thought it served Geoffroi.

stages.title: The Lady of the Manor
stages.clues: Ysabeau turns to the covenant. If Geoffroi finds out, he may have an astrologer judge her daily, send her to Normandy, have her silenced by magic, or threaten to take her daughters (Ant p. 19).

stages.title: The Peasants' Revolt
stages.clues: Anger spills over into neighboring lands, fed by demons of resentment, ambition and jealousy, and one of the covenant's companions, possessed, plans and leads the mob. A manor house, a mill and a chapel go first, then the farms and granaries the peasants need most (Ant p. 18).
stages.ignored: The covenant gains the War Zone External Relations Hook (Covenants p. 22).

neighbours.secrets:
Geoffroi begins as a reasonable man and a possible ally, grows obsessed, and ends a danger to himself, his vassals and his neighbors. He sees little difference between Divine, Faerie, Magic and Infernal, fills his woods with beasts from afar and his court with magicians. The story has two sides, his research and the neglect of his lands, and the book advises at least one story from each stage. Many stages can serve as news brought by infiltration, intrigue or scrying (Ant p. 14). The Infernal and Parma stages can be braided with the Divine Abbot's story (Ant p. 113).

Investigating (Ant p. 18): the troubles plainly lead to his court; what remains is why, who holds his ear, and how to end it. Infiltrating the council can be done openly, but it will expect its members to do the baron's wishes, which an oath may forbid. Spying or scrying shows the alliances and plots kept out of the chamber, and can split the council. Arcane Connections taken from people or rooms allow listening in, or worse.

Endings (Ant pp. 19-21). Let sleeping dogs lie: he loses his lands, signing whatever he is handed, and dies poor, while nobles and Guillaume fight over them, Ysabeau and her daughters go back to Arques, and the war or the wizards become the covenant's problem. Persuade him: threaten his family, expose François, take the council's place with proof of its treachery, or send rivals, friends or the Church to turn him. Eliminate him, if an heir is of age, or leave him infirm under a regent: the Code forbids it, the court wizards may trace it, and Ysabeau and the heir must then be guarded from them. Persuade the wizards to leave, by threats, bribes or a fair sharing of learning. Eliminate the wizards, perhaps through Tremere, Flambeau or Hoplites, and expect their traditions' revenge and the baron's own, by trade and fear. Induct them into Ex Miscellanea, under the Oath. Or found a rival order with a code of its own, which House Tremere would oppose, and which could become the great question of the next Grand Tribunal.

Interference: whether acting against a hedge wizard is meddling with mundanes has no fixed answer. Each case goes to Tribunal, for the magi to argue and not for the troupe to rule (Ant p. 19).

neighbours.name: The Ambitious Medicus
neighbours.summary: An itinerant doctor settles happily into the baron's court.
neighbours.secrets: Skilled in the elemental arts, he tilts the court's humors toward the sanguine, so that all think him a friend, even as the baron's riches begin to vanish. Only the phlegmatic steward suspects, and looks for someone who will listen (Ant p. 13).

neighbours.name: The Magical Swordsmith
neighbours.summary: The baron asks that his swordsmith be let work at the covenant.
neighbours.secrets: A peasant craftsman, daunted by the wealthy and the Gifted, who needs the covenant's beneficial air. Can the magi learn from him, and will they send him back to Geoffroi or keep him for another use (Ant p. 15)?

neighbours.name: The Stolen Ring
neighbours.summary: A Jewish goldsmith and his apprentice ask the magi's help.
neighbours.secrets: A ring he burned magic into for Baron Geoffroi has been stolen. He fears the baron's wrath and that it will serve as an Arcane Connection to him. Where is it, what does the thief intend, and what is the apprentice's part (Ant p. 22)?

neighbours.name: The Baron's Overlord
neighbours.summary: The great lord whose favored vassal Baron Le Cornu is, a count here but an earl or duke in other lands: the Count of Champagne in the Normandy Tribunal, the Earl of Chester in Cheshire, and so on. He can raise an army of thousands if he must, and the baron and his family can shelter at his court.
neighbours.secrets:
He expects the baron to handle his own troubles, since the baron holds his place by being useful. He cares far less about the magi: the Order has never overthrown a count, and one covenant's land and soldiers would mean little to him. He has more to gain from their friendship than to lose by leaving them be, as the baron knows, and that restrains the baron (Ant p. 26).

He can defuse a quarrel, sending emissaries to broker a truce if raids break out, or to tell over-aggressive magi to stand down or meet his army. He values the baron and his knights above anything the covenant has, and will order an end to a futile war (Ant pp. 26, 34). Keep him from being drawn in too far: he is too strong for most covenants to resist (Ant p. 26).

neighbours.name: Le Cornu's Keep
neighbours.summary: The baron's tower keep, on the richest of his manors, about ten miles and half a day's ride from the covenant. A chapel stands beside it, and a permanent guard of dismounted men-at-arms holds it.
neighbours.secrets:
Once he knows wizards can fly or turn into birds, the baron keeps his chamber shuttered tight, hangs bells on the doors of sensitive rooms, and orders patrols at random hours of the night. His people demand a password before any unusual order, and watch for anyone acting out of place, since magic can change a face. They avoid the eyes of magi, on account of Entrancement (ArM5 p. 65), and take suspected wizards blindfolded and gagged to the dungeon (Ant p. 30).

These measures are guesswork with gaps. He knows little of Arcane Connections and takes no care over a shed hair or a favorite cloak (Ant p. 30). All this makes it somewhat hard to slip a magical spy inside (Ant p. 31).

neighbours.name: The Barony of Le Cornu
neighbours.summary:
A minor barony of about ten manors, won by the young Giraud as his reward when his father's rising was put down. They were gathered one at a time, so they lie scattered: at least one borders the covenant, and others may be days away. Vassal knights run most of them. It has good woodland, and may hold a mill, a bridge, a road or a market.

The baron spends about half his time at his keep; the rest goes on visiting his manors and attending his lord's court. A steward travels among the estates in his absence, and if he died before his eldest son came of age, his brother Sir Artur would rule as steward.
neighbours.secrets:
The father was dispossessed or killed, as suits the saga. The manors by the covenant came with the barony, or later as a spur to continued loyalty (Ant p. 24).

The baron may own the main road to the covenant, and the land under some of its vis sources (Ant p. 27).

neighbours.name: The Le Cornu Family
neighbours.summary: The baron, Lady Éloise and their four children, two sons and two daughters, all under ten, with the baron's brother Sir Artur. They can take refuge at the count's court.
neighbours.secrets: The sons are 9 and 6 when the conflict starts, and enter the circle of trust at 21 (Ant p. 29). The children are not named.

neighbours.name: The Baron's Retainers
neighbours.summary: The men who serve Baron Le Cornu: a mesnie of three household knights; nine vassal knights, Sir Artur among them; two household squires, one of them Bertrand Gallain; another fifteen mounted men-at-arms, counting all his knights' squires; twelve dismounted men-at-arms who guard the castle; and about fifty half-trained peasant levies for emergencies. A confessor and a steward complete the household.

details.rules: The household knights use the Knight companion template (ArM5 p. 23), without the Relic Virtue or the Overconfident Flaw. The castle guard use the Standard Soldier grog template (ArM5 p. 22) (Ant p. 24).

neighbours.secrets: In open war he holds at least half his knights at home and raids with a dozen riders: himself, three knights and eight men-at-arms (Ant p. 31). His men soon weary of guard duty, so a guard is only ever a short-term measure (Ant p. 27).

neighbours.name: Folk Who Deal With the Covenant
neighbours.summary: Farmers, artisans and others who deal with the covenant, with nothing to show that anything ties them together.

details.rules: One season for the first three agents, all outside the covenant. After that, one season for each outsider, two or more for a lowly covenfolk, and more than two for anyone of higher importance (Ant p. 29). The agency rules of Houses of Hermes: Societates pp. 140-144 can guide who he recruits, and serve players who want agents of their own (Ant p. 28).

neighbours.secrets:
A network of spies and informers gathered as relations sour, run for the baron by one of his inner circle, probably his wife. It starts with people loosely tied to the covenant, such as farmers and artisans who deliver there, and with anyone who bears it a grudge: thwarted apprentices, evicted tenants, rival magi, cheated merchants. Later it seeks covenfolk or grogs open to bribery or extortion, such as those with poor relatives or a weakness for drink or dice (Ant pp. 28-29).

Each agent reports small things, and over time the baron assembles a surprisingly full account of the covenant: its defenses, members, quarrels, income and spending (Ant p. 29). The storyguide need only keep a list of how many there are and roughly where (Ant p. 29).

Those inside the covenant are the easiest to expose, with Intellego Mentem spells, and the hardest to replace, but random checks hurt morale and may drive the unhappy to him; under the loyalty rules of Covenants, a magical questioning is probably a minor humiliation. Those outside are hard to trace. An exposed agent can be turned, fed false news, bribed, frightened or avoided, and a thorough covenant can destroy the network, over many stories (Ant pp. 31-32). The baron may also try to recruit a player's own grog or companion (Ant p. 32).

neighbours.name: The Keep's Chapel
neighbours.summary: The castle chapel beside the baron's keep, served by Brother Henri Raoullin.
neighbours.secrets: The baron's diary lies hidden under the altar, where he wrongly believes no magic can find it (Ant p. 29).

neighbours.name: The Baron's Relics
neighbours.summary: A rich and growing collection of relics, some carried on the baron's person. Every stranger at his court must touch or kiss one before he will see them.
neighbours.secrets: All of them are fakes. He has come to believe the touch of a relic dispels any magic, and spends much time and money on them. This and his other odd habits give him a local Reputation as Eccentric within a few years (Ant p. 30). His Church Lore specialty is relics, for all the good it does him (Ant p. 25).

neighbours.name: The Baron and the Covenant
neighbours.summary: A new lord holds the manor next door, and he has begun asking who the covenant's liege is and by what right it keeps armed men.

stages.title: A Squire Comes Calling
stages.clues: Bertrand Gallain arrives to meet the new neighbors, asking who their liege is and why they keep armed men.
stages.ignored: Careless answers tell the baron what disturbs him: Gifted magi look like villains, admitted magic suggests heresy, and a castle or grogs without leave from a high lord upset him greatly. He asks to visit, and either way starts seeking agents (Ant p. 27).
stages.turned: If he visits, he is plainly suspicious, and presses to know who gave them the right to their home and their soldiers.

stages.title: A Letter About Trespass
stages.clues: Covenant folk are seen on his land, armed or not, and a written warning arrives (Ant p. 27).
stages.ignored: If they keep coming, for vis or anything else, he forbids it, has them watched, and then sets a guard or goes to law. A spy may tail them; he won't know what vis is, but sees it matters, and bargains with it (Ant pp. 27-28).

stages.title: Favors and Gifts
stages.clues: While relations are good he sends fine gifts, such as dishes, garments, hounds and horses, and hints that enchanted gifts would be a fitting return (Ant p. 27).
stages.ignored: He is insulted if none come, and offended if refused a favor such as battle magic before his lord's war.
stages.turned: He cannot detect magic, so a placebo will do for a while. In time he asks for what cannot be faked: saving his crops from blight, or magic to hunt down rebels.

stages.title: Closed Roads
stages.clues: At odds with the covenant, he bars it from his woods, mills, bridges, roads and markets. That may mean the main way in, and vis sources on his land (Ant p. 27).

stages.title: A Summons
stages.clues: A lawsuit: use only one or two, as repeated suits grow dull (Ant p. 28).
stages.ignored: Trespass carries a small fine. What matters is answering: defying the summons angers him into a new plot.
stages.stopped: If they come to court he relaxes somewhat, win or lose, for they have shown respect for mundane authority.
stages.turned: Removing something valuable makes it burglary, perhaps a hanging matter, in royal court a few seasons off. A challenge to the covenant's title must be brought by the count, unless a tame noble holds it, but the baron argues it himself, even against an allod. If his case is strong he offers to settle, with extra demands (Ant pp. 28, 34).

stages.title: Eyes and Ears
stages.clues: Delivery men ask too many questions, and shadowy figures are seen near restricted parts of the covenant (Ant pp. 28-29, 32).
stages.stopped: Exposing agents is among the best ways to halt him, though he can replace them.

stages.title: Friends Turned Away
stages.clues: Friends of the covenant grow cold. He beats his own villeins for visiting, sends squires or knights to frighten the lower orders, and threatens to boycott merchants. Priests and abbots hear that magi are wicked, with bribes or veiled threats and the risk of a bad Reputation or the bishop's displeasure (Ant p. 29).
stages.ignored: The covenant weakens and may seek a new mundane patron, as he hopes: his overlord.
stages.stopped: A story can win a friend back, such as grogs scaring off a bullying squire.

stages.title: Sowing Discord
stages.clues: His wife or confessor meets a malcontent in secret, listing the magi's failings and praising the peace to be had (Ant pp. 29-30).
stages.ignored: Unless the troupe wants treachery, he should fail at real infighting: at worst he gains a few agents or some deserters.

stages.title: Old Enemies at the Keep
stages.clues: Hedge wizards the magi insulted, or a suspicious clergyman, are summoned to his keep and given a sympathetic ear. Foes the covenant thought beaten may return, and in a high fantasy saga he may pact with faeries or magical beasts (Ant p. 30).

stages.title: The Burglar
stages.clues: After a defeat by the magi, or if he suspects witchcraft, he seeks a specialist. That may take seasons or years, and may mean forgiving a crime. Agents inside let him in, keep watch and aid his escape (Ant p. 30).
stages.ignored: He takes something small, such as a lab text or charged item, not a high summa or an invested device, and rushes it to the baron.
stages.stopped: Give the players a chance to catch him: a good story for grogs.

stages.title: Held for Ransom
stages.clues: If the covenant breaks into his keep, fights his men or threatens him, he hears from agents where its members will be and has knights lay an ambush to take prisoners, not to kill. A character accused of a serious crime may be held for trial (Ant pp. 30-31).
stages.turned: He frees prisoners for restitution or a formal agreement. Coin alone will not do; a promise must come with it.

stages.title: Torch and Sword
stages.clues: He or his successor attacks if his life is threatened, or he dies or falls under a spell without explanation; his advisers need no proof (Ant p. 31).
stages.ignored: He fortifies the near manors and raids. His first targets are vis sources he knows of, then wooden bridges and mills, then property, and he kills or drives off farmers and laborers. Expect lasting financial harm.
stages.stopped: See Ending the fighting in the secrets.

stages.title: Terms, and the Tribunal's Answer
stages.clues: Peace comes by capitulation, relocation or treaty (Ant pp. 34-35).
stages.ignored: Swearing fealty to the count ends the quarrel and may win an ally, but breaks the Peripheral Code in every Tribunal, since it is a pledge of personal service like a court wizard's. It must then be kept secret from other magi. A companion made a figurehead vassal will not fool him (Ant p. 34).
stages.stopped: Moving the covenant is extreme and lets him win, but a change of setting can suit a troupe (Ant pp. 34-35).
stages.turned: A treaty that stops short of personal service, beginning perhaps with non-aggression and growing as disputes arise. It then raises questions at Tribunal: who owns vis on his land, whether the covenant could give it away or bind other magi, whether it should have been ratified, whether the magi have become court wizards, and how far magi must obey mundane law. Rulings may be narrow or sweeping, reach the Grand Tribunal, or assert that magi may only be tried in Hermetic courts (Ant pp. 35-36; HoH:TL p. 51; in Normandy, The Lion and the Lily pp. 24-25).

neighbours.secrets:
By fair means or foul, the baron means to end the magi's independence and bring them to swear fealty, which the Code forbids. He knows he cannot beat a typical covenant by force, and the Code lets magi defend themselves against mundanes (HoH:TL p. 51), so he uses carrot and stick. Lean too far toward him and the magi risk a charge of meddling with mundanes; rebuff him too often and he turns to harassment. Either way there are stories (Ant p. 27). The stages are the book's plots in its order; pick those that fit, as his next step depends on what the magi do.

A vis source on his land counts as the Contested Resources Hook: reveal a Hidden Hook as this, or add a new one with a new Boon to balance it, or give the covenant a new resource worth the same build points (Ant p. 28).

Jurisdiction (Ant pp. 32-33). The baron's own court hears small cases such as trespass, so he both sues and judges. He takes that seriously, and strong evidence can win there as anywhere. If the players find that unfair, say such cases go to his overlord's court here. Land, economic privileges and capital crimes go to royal court, and stealing livestock or poaching big game can mean death. A Church court hears clergy, and most inheritance and contract cases. Secular courts are described in Lords of Men pp. 80-82, Church courts in The Church pp. 35-36.

Arguing a case (Ant pp. 32-34). The Gift sets any secular court against magi, who may earn a bad local Reputation by appearing, Gentle Gift aside. No one is presumed innocent or protected against incriminating himself; testimony counts more than things. Character witnesses matter, and in a canon court enough clergy clear the accused outright (compurgation). Eyewitnesses weigh heavily, but alternative explanations can answer them. Land cases turn on long possession, and parish records are the best proof. Benefit of clergy is open: rule that magi do not count unless ordained, or leave it unsettled and make a story of it.

Stolen vis (Ant p. 34). If the vis is in something of value, a jewel or a large beast, the court tries an ordinary theft. If it is in something cheap, the baron cannot show its worth without a magus to testify, so the verdict is trespass; but he persuades the court that taking the same thing again proves its value, and any repeat is serious burglary.

Land verdicts (Ant p. 34). A covenant with the Autocephalous Boon (Covenants p. 20) wins outright. Otherwise it must settle by owning the count as lord and taking a charter, or argue in royal court, where a win gives it that Boon. If it loses, the land reverts to the count, and after a week the baron comes with armed men to clear the squatters.

Ending the fighting (Ant p. 34). A couple of raids beaten off, a manor sacked, or two or three knights killed or badly hurt make him ask for a truce; a captured knight or adviser brings a truce and a ransom. Too great a show of force drives him to a last decisive battle.

His demands, most important first (Ant p. 35): no attacks on the count or his vassals and no spells on them unasked, self-defense excepted; proof the magi's powers are not Infernal, such as taking confession and communion; magical service to his liege, which breaks the Code and which he can be argued out of; respect for his bounds, with nothing taken unpaid, vis included, and he prefers payment in enchantments or spells; obedience to mundane law, handing over the accused and answering lawsuits, the court being negotiable; a share of income from anything they cannot prove is theirs; the count's leave to keep men-at-arms, or disarm; and scutage, which he will waive to gain a higher demand. If they agree to all, he has no more quarrel.

What the count grants in return, most valuable first (Ant p. 35): recognition that the covenant owns its land and resources, its serfs included; a charter making it an independent legal body; leave for an armed garrison; exemption from military service and scutage; exclusive rights to vis on the baron's lands; leave to clear wasteland; leave to hunt magical beasts; and exemption from some taxes and fines. A settlement with the count is final.

neighbours.name: The Papal Curia
neighbours.summary: The pope's court at Rome. Under Innocent III and, since his death in 1216, Honorius III, it has worked to reform the Church and draw power to itself. To speak to a legate is to speak to the pope, and an attack on one is as good as an attack on him.
neighbours.secrets:
Bringing the Order under Rome would be a great prize, and a widespread pseudo-religious order outside papal authority is bad politics: the monastic orders might wonder if they too could do without Rome. Other Church factions may oppose the mission (Ant pp. 38-39). The curia knows of the Societas of the Mystical Christ, and Father Joseph's books circulate there (Ant pp. 42, 45).

The papacy has no sound way to prove its letters: seals can be forged, despite harsh penalties (Ant p. 43).

neighbours.name: Napoli
neighbours.summary: Father Joseph's birthplace, where his family still live. Few there, outside perhaps the bishop's court, have more than a vague idea of his mission.

neighbours.name: San Giovanni Maggiore
neighbours.summary: The church in Napoli where Joseph was a canon and wrote his books on the Order of Hermes between 1203 and 1210. He is well known there.

neighbours.name: The Family of Father Joseph
neighbours.summary: Poor folk of Napoli, simple fishermen for the most part, with several relatives in the lower clergy.
neighbours.secrets: He keeps them out of his talk to protect them from unscrupulous magi; he would put his mission first if they were threatened (Ant p. 42).

neighbours.name: The Societas of the Mystical Christ
neighbours.summary: A Hermetic societas of Christian magi, with chapters across the Tribunals, that discusses a closer union of the Order and the Church. It is no secret, but few have heard of it.

details.rules: Open to any Christian magus, however devout; pagans, Muslims and Jews must convert and be baptized first. It is a political faction, not a Mystery Cult, and grants no magical benefit or cost (Ant pp. 44-45). It has a chapter in each Tribunal. Its sign is the chi-rho, followed by the astrological sign for mercury.
details.wants: A religious Order of Hermes under a Grand Master and the pope.
details.offers: Standing among those high in the Church who know of it: a member who names it in a petition to the curia (The Church pp. 46-48) has +3 to his Petition Total. Low-ranking clergy will not have heard of it.

neighbours.secrets:
It was founded at Father Joseph's suggestion, though he is no magus, no member, and not its master. He meets its leaders at least once a year, knows who belongs, and may seek its help if threatened. It spreads his ideas and is the seed of his new Order: he expects the first Grand Master to come from its leaders, and lets it claim his ideas as its own (Ant pp. 44-45). It looks into the writings and deeds of pious magi as possible recruits (Ant p. 45).

The book names no member, and the troupe sets its size and power to suit the saga (Ant p. 49). In a saga that wants it, an inner circle may hold Mystery scripts for Divine Virtues (Ant p. 45), or it may be a cabal of power-mad Tytalus magi, with Father Joseph their pawn since his days as a notary (Ant p. 49).

Other possible allies (Ant p. 45): in the Rhine, it might work as a Gild (Guardians of the Forests p. 27) with the olive as its tree, or the Apple Gild may join him; in Thebes, a League might serve. The Priory of Saint Nerius (RoP:D p. 94) and the covenant of Cunfin (The Lion and the Lily p. 106) may also side with him.

neighbours.name: The Legate's Mission
neighbours.summary: A papal legate is going from covenant to covenant, asking magi to consider joining the Order to the Church.

stages.title: Discussion and Travel
stages.clues: He goes from covenant to covenant talking, settling for seasons where regular meetings help, and courts the Tribunal's influential magi so that they spread his ideas (Ant p. 44).
stages.ignored: He gathers the sites of more covenants, and would love to ride with a Redcap. He uses Redcaps for his letters if allowed, and looks to clerical gossip when he runs out of known covenants.

stages.title: The Societas Grows
stages.clues: Chapters of the Societas of the Mystical Christ appear in the Tribunals, and investigators ask after pious magi's characters (Ant pp. 44-45).

stages.title: Hermetic Benefices
stages.clues: Covenants are offered tithes as a monastery holds them, keeping most, paying a parish priest, and sending a little to the bishop (Ant pp. 45-46; The Church pp. 41-43).
stages.ignored: Magi come to care about their parishes, and their covenants take a place like a monastery's among their neighbors.
stages.turned: Magi can create wealth anyway, but the standing is useful: Church backing lets a covenant turn down nobles who ask for magic.

stages.title: Synods and Tribunals
stages.clues: Bishops and archdeacons invite local magi to synods (The Church p. 45), and he urges magi to ask bishops and abbots to Tribunals and councils as non-voting speakers or observers (Ant p. 46).
stages.ignored: He can call special synods, but wants ties that outlast him.

stages.title: The Bishop's Court
stages.clues: Once relations are good, bishops' courts ask magi to help verify miracles and find facts in canon crimes (Ant pp. 46-47).
stages.turned: He wants a court-wizard charge brought, once sure his allies will carry it, and a Peripheral Code ruling that this is no crime. A second-best outcome is a precedent making it a lesser crime with a small vis fine.

stages.title: Conversion and Baptism
stages.clues: He debates pagans and infidels and urges baptism. He uses no threats, knowing they would backfire, and will not be distracted from the whole Order by a few souls (Ant p. 47).

stages.title: The Grand Master
stages.clues: The Order must rally behind one Grand Master (Ant pp. 47-48).
stages.ignored: He prefers a vote of the Grand Tribunal, then a regional Tribunal's choice that forces the others to choose, then a Societas leader declaring himself, and last a papal appointment. Rome does not care how the choice is made, only that most magi accept it; he suggests the archmages elect one at each Grand Tribunal, as cardinals elect a pope.
stages.turned: A Grand Master seen as illegitimate invites certamen and Wizard's War.

stages.title: A Religious Order
stages.clues: The pope recognizes the title and the Order, likely by bull, and the Grand Master accepts his authority. An agreed Peripheral Code goes out as the new Order's canon rules, and it goes on governing itself much as before (Ant pp. 37, 48).
stages.ignored: In time those who refuse are Marched. Later generations may push it toward monastic ways: separate magi and magae, set prayers, an end to violence as a legal tool.

neighbours.secrets:
Father Joseph attacks no one; he sets the Order against itself, and politics may end in violence or a new Schism War (Ant p. 7). Decide how far he has come before the characters meet him: he may have few Hermetic allies, or many converts already (Ant p. 41). The stages are the book's strategies in its order.

First meetings (Ant pp. 41-42). He seeks an audience at a covenant he knows of, or meets the magi as another covenant's guest. He may prefer a nearby parish church, sending a messenger, since spilling blood in a sanctuary is a canon crime that might give even hostile magi pause. He may be met on the road, as a rumor from friends or foes, or at Tribunal with a large faction behind him.

Finding him out (Ant pp. 42, 46). Roll on the Reputation Ease Factor Table (ArM5 p. 19) to know him as Pompius's notary, or as a legate; any Church Lore tells what a legate is. Few magi remember him, while he remembers them well. Only magi with strong Church contacts will have noticed his books.

If the Order is secretive, say how he got away (Ant pp. 40-41): he was thought dead in Pompius's spectacular Twilight; the local magi were lax; he was never let go, and is the pawn of a faction; or a miracle saved him or his memories.

Ridicule (Ant p. 48). Many magi laugh, and he answers that Rome was a pagan capital once. Ignoring him avoids blame but works only for a while, since not every magus will.

Befuddlement (Ant p. 48). Mentem magic can destroy his mind or his purpose, but if the papacy means it, a new legate comes, and a miracle may restore him. Tampering with the pope means the curia too, again and again, at the risk of a miracle, a charge of mundane interference and the Church's wrath.

Enlistment (Ant p. 48). Magi who join may be asked to guard him or travel seeking converts, and may maneuver for terms or the Grand Mastership, at the risk of charges of endangering the Order.

In the East (Ant pp. 48-49). Orthodox magi may refuse him, though Latin crusaders in the east are likely to back a papal Order. Greek fathers may raise a rival Order; one Grand Master may balance between Rome and Constantinople, or Latin and Greek Masters may stand side by side.

Dominion (Ant p. 49). If Rome can have a Grand Master, might a magus become pope? Ambitious magi may see the way.

Enemies of his enemies (Ant p. 49). Bishop Orris and other churchmen, perhaps some of the curia, may work with magi against him, and noble courts fear a pope with wizards at his command. Old foes may ally.

Martyrdom (Ant p. 49). He can be killed, though a miracle may save him. At best a new legate follows, guarded by the military orders, with the Societas behind him. At worst the papacy wanted this, and preaches crusade: the military orders answer at once, and minor nobles would come for the lands of tame nobles called heretics. A major lord like Frederick II might use it to meet his own crusade vow close to home. The killers face Tribunal for interference, and mundane justice besides. If martyred he becomes a saint, perhaps patron of wizards, and works on (RoP:D pp. 85-89).

Scaling him (Ant p. 49). Add Faith to the relic, choose his allies' power, and set how warmly the Church backs him. For a very high-level saga, a Grand Master has already been proclaimed, and the Order must submit or split.

neighbours.name: Miracle of the Magi
neighbours.summary: The local clergy are talking of wonders.
neighbours.secrets: Local clergy see the magi cast spells, and the dean writes to the curia asking guidance. The letter reaches Father Joseph, who recognizes Hermetic magic and comes to the deanery to find them (Ant p. 44).

neighbours.name: Host of the Church
neighbours.summary: The covenant is asked to house a preaching guest.
neighbours.secrets: Sympathetic magi let Father Joseph stay for seasons, and Christian magi from all over the Tribunal come to hear him, with retinues to house. Then argumentative pagan magi arrive; Father Joseph stays calm, but malicious certamen follows, and unless someone calms things, Wizard's War or murder (Ant p. 44).

neighbours.name: Pilgrimage
neighbours.summary: A legate wants a magus to travel with him.
neighbours.secrets: Father Joseph picks a magus who opposes him, though not a homicidal one, to travel the Tribunal with him, hoping to win him by argument and example. The magus may be accused of revealing hidden covenants, if that is a crime, and may have to defend him from pagans (Ant p. 44).

neighbours.name: The Address
neighbours.summary: A churchman wants to speak at Tribunal.
neighbours.secrets: Father Joseph wants to propose a treaty and a religious Rule at Tribunal, where custom usually lets only magi speak. Allies argue his right or speak for him; foes block or answer him. He waits for a meeting where he has support; a significant minority publicly backing him is his second-best result, and without either he tries the next Tribunal (Ant p. 44).

neighbours.name: Christ Underground
neighbours.summary: Christian magi in a pagan Tribunal are growing wary.
neighbours.secrets: Where pagans or other anti-papal magi rule the Tribunal, the Societas must hide from concerted Wizard's War, moving Father Joseph from one safe house to the next as he preaches, glad of the likeness to the early Church; a martyr or two is no disaster. The magi may hide him, support their brothers across a border, or be sent to hunt him (Ant p. 45).

neighbours.name: The Good News
neighbours.summary: Someone is asking about the good character of local magi.
neighbours.secrets: The Societas recruits pious magi on its own account. Members may be asked to vouch for neighbors; others may stumble on its agents at this work (Ant p. 45).

neighbours.name: First Rights
neighbours.summary: The bishop has a gift for the covenant.
neighbours.secrets: On the pope's order the bishop gives the covenant several benefices, a Typical Income Source, taken from a chapter of canons he thinks too strong. The outraged canons, of the diocese's second church, make bitter enemies; refusing makes one of the bishop (Ant p. 46).

neighbours.name: Care of Souls
neighbours.summary: The covenant needs a priest for its new parish.
neighbours.secrets: With a benefice the magi must hire a priest, who then comes to them for help: sick farm animals, a lost child, a lie between merchants (Ant p. 46).

neighbours.name: The Tithe
neighbours.summary: It is time to assess the parish's crops.
neighbours.secrets: The magi or their agents must go round the parish yearly to assess each field's yield, a clerk's usual job and a chance to seek vis. A tithe that counted natural vis in the produce would be an easy gain (Ant p. 46).

neighbours.name: Slanderous Accusations
neighbours.summary: The bishop invites the magi to a synod.
neighbours.secrets: Slander has been a canon crime since 1215. A bishop who thinks magic no evil learns his priests preach that magi serve the devil, and calls a synod, inviting the magi to show otherwise (Ant p. 46).

neighbours.name: Heretics
neighbours.summary: The rural dean invites the magi to a synod.
neighbours.secrets: The dean near the covenant and some of his priests have fallen into heresy, perhaps Catharism, as the magi see at his synod. Report it and they may have to help reform or suppress him; ignore it and they may be accused themselves when the bishop finds out (Ant p. 46).

neighbours.name: Opulent Council Chambers
neighbours.summary: The bishop's deacon has come to the covenant's council.
neighbours.secrets: A severely ascetic deacon, at the covenant's yearly council, is shocked by its wealth. The bishop writes asking its sources of income, from curiosity, a hope of gifts, or his deacon's concern (Ant p. 46).

neighbours.name: Authentic Miracles
neighbours.summary: A holy man in a village is said to heal lepers.
neighbours.secrets: The bishop asks the magi if a village holy man who heals lepers who pray and fast with him is a true conduit of miracles, a charlatan, or a wizard of some kind (Ant p. 47).

neighbours.name: Possession
neighbours.summary: A family lies murdered on the cathedral steps.
neighbours.secrets: In a hot, still summer a Jewish family is murdered on the cathedral steps one Sunday evening, and no one knows by whom. Fearing demons in the townsfolk and a pogrom to come, the bishop asks the magi to investigate and deliver the town (Ant p. 47).

neighbours.name: The River Jordan
neighbours.summary: A legate is baptizing magi on the Danube.
neighbours.secrets: Father Joseph sets up a mission at a covenant on the Danube, offering baptism in the river as John did. Pagan magi come to be baptized, pursued by the jealous animal spirits of their cult. The magi may be hosts facing the spirits, or the converts defeating their old gods (Ant p. 47).

neighbours.name: Order and Anti-Order
neighbours.summary: Rival Grand Masters divide the Order.
neighbours.secrets: Rome and Normandy proclaim rival Grand Masters. Father Joseph asks respected magi to broker a peace, since the papacy could settle it but cannot tell who has the most support. A player's character may be one of the rivals (Ant p. 48).

neighbours.name: The Lady Chapel of St. John's
neighbours.summary: The cathedral's Lady Chapel, where the Divine aura is at its strongest.

neighbours.name: The Cathedral Chapter of St. John
neighbours.summary: The nine canons of St. John's, who care for the cathedral and sing its plainchant under the provost, Father Peter. The choir's music fills the congregation with wonder at God, or whatever feeling suits the Mass, and it has made the cathedral famous. Some canons feel snubbed at being left out of Brother Theodoric's circle of singers.
neighbours.secrets:
Five of the nine, Theodoric among them, are a Holy Tradition of Cantores (RoP: The Divine Revised Edition pp. 93-94), who worship through plainchant. The other four, Father Peter among them, sometimes join their group ceremonies. Their favored Abilities are Holy Music, Invocation, Blessing and Enchanting Music; they use the last to move the congregation (p. 53).

Orris knows what they can do and is in awe of their faith. He has rarely asked for their miracles, trusting Theodoric's piety. In thanks for this, the chapter has blessed his health in a yearly ritual for 10 years: +5 to his aging rolls (Holy Music / Blessing 50), and the source of his Warping.

Ceremony totals (p. 53): Theodoric leading the four Cantores adds +24 to miraculous effects (the Cantores' Presence + Holy Music). The full nine, unled, add +46 (+25 group bonus, -9 participants, +30 from the Cantores' and canons' Presence + Holy Music). By Invocation instead of Holy Music, the bonus from Communication + Invocation is +14 led and +16 unled.

The block of specialists gives the 4 Cantores Ceremony 5 (p. 52), an Ability not among the favored ones of p. 53.

neighbours.name: The Friars Preacher
neighbours.summary: Three black-habited Dominican friars lent to the diocese by the local chapter house, and models of good conduct. They preach by turns in market squares and alehouses, moving on every few nights. Their theme is God's hatred of idolaters and sorcerers, whom they put beside murderers, adulterers, perjurers and fornicators.

details.rules: They travel together and preach by turns, drink little, eat frugally, and stay only a few nights in each town or village.
details.wants: To turn hearts from idolatry and sin, and to expose the sorcerers named to them.

neighbours.secrets:
The Order of St. Dominic was founded to fight heresy, and Orris asks for these three once his inquiries are done (p. 59). They call magicians fraudsters who fake miracles, sinners against Nature and God, and idolaters who call on demons. They name the player magi outright, using whatever Orris has found, but they are honest: they do not embellish or lie. On preachers, see Art & Academe pp. 13-14.

Their statistics are not printed. Base them on the Franciscan friar of RoP: The Divine Revised Edition p. 96, with Profession: Preacher in place of Teaching, and perhaps a Puissant Virtue in it (p. 59). Finding them may take several days of following their trail (p. 59).

Reputation (p. 59): their campaign gives everyone identified with the covenant's magic a bad Reputation of 1, its nature varying by person. Each identifiable event adds an experience point, and so does each season of preaching; it rises as an Ability (ArM5 p. 167). It hurts business in the diocese and the covenfolk's loyalty (Covenants p. 40).

Against them (p. 64): a public clash rallies the locals against the attacker, and three mysterious deaths feed the rumours. Orris sends replacements, who raise Reputation at half the rate, these three being the order's best. If deaths go on, their superior eventually refuses to send more.

Debate (p. 64): a formal challenge draws wide attention, and the bad Reputation gains no experience that season; an ad hoc debate does not give this. Rules are in Houses of Hermes: Societates p. 90 and Art & Academe p. 104. The friars keep to academic disputatio; magi may range wider but suffer The Gift's penalty. A win earns a good Reputation of 1 that counters the bad, possibly for the others too. A loss still stops the rise that season; a botch adds a point. Later debates earn 1 experience each, and only one debate a season counts.

Scripture they may quote (p. 60): Wisdom 17:7; Exodus 22:18; Leviticus 19:31 and 20:27; Deuteronomy 18:10-12; 1 Samuel 15:23; Isaiah 47:13-14; Micah 5:12-13; Malachi 3:5; Galatians 5:19-21; Revelation 21:8 and 22:14-15.

neighbours.name: The Church Knights
neighbours.summary: Whichever military order keeps the nearest commandery: the Order of Santiago in Iberia, the Teutonic Order, working from Hungary, in eastern Europe, and the Knights Templar nearly everywhere else. They are veterans of war, of sieges above all.

details.wants: To fight pagans and infidels, as the pope charges them, and to aid a bishop who asks with the authority of his rank.

neighbours.secrets:
The commander has Leadership 5, direct experience in the Holy Land and siege engineers who can undermine a fortress; he leads his force as a trained group (p. 62).

Numbers (p. 62): at least five knights beyond the commander, and a dozen or more sergeants, sized to the covenant's strength before any desertions: at least as many sergeants as the turb had grogs, and as many knights as there are companions.

Statistics (p. 62): The Church pp. 126-127. Otherwise, knights are the Knight companion template (ArM5 p. 23), sergeants the Standard Soldier (ArM5 p. 22), and the leader of each trained group of five a Grizzled Veteran (ArM5 p. 21). Each knight very likely has a relic of Faith 1 or more. Mass warfare and sieges: Lords of Men pp. 109-116.

This is the generic force of the story. Sagas with a Tribunal pack may already hold the order itself.

neighbours.name: Bishop Orris's War on Sorcery
neighbours.summary: The covenant lies in Bishop Orris's diocese, and he has been hard on sorcerers before. He is a just man, much loved by his flock.

stages.title: The Visitation
stages.clues: Every year a bishop must inspect his parishes, and Orris usually leaves this to his archdeacon, who skips the remote ones. The archdeacon has fallen ill, so the bishop comes himself. Word reaches the covenant that a summoner, a sub-deacon paid by the accused, has called someone to the bishop's court for sorcery. The accused may be a farmer who sells to the covenant, a past servant, a grog's relative, a Dependent or True Love, or a magus notorious for a crime.
stages.ignored: The bishop arrives in mid-afternoon with his secretary, four acolytes and four hired guards, ten in all (more in lawless country), and the parish holds a feast. A magus or companion of standing may be asked to sit at his table, and the fateful meeting may happen there.
stages.turned: Intelligence + Organization Lore: Church against Ease Factor 9 shows his retinue is unusually small, for two or three times as many are allowed and can ruin a parish.

stages.title: The Bishop's Court
stages.clues: He holds court in the parish church the next day, on a platform before the altar, with a notary and Deacon Adam. He prays for justice and wisdom, tempering the Dominion aura toward Justice, which aids all efforts to uncover secrets. After the checklist of parish duties he tries the small cases (brawling in church, missed festivals, a birth seven months after a wedding) with warnings, small fines and public penance, fairly and without undue leniency.
stages.ignored: If he senses magic on the accused he blanches, speaks hotly of the danger of sorcery, then resorts to compurgation, since he will not convict on hearsay. With fewer than 12 oath-takers on the Bible he convicts: public penance such as a white sheet before the congregation, a fine, or, for a major crime done by magic, the secular courts.
stages.stopped: Twelve people swear to the accused's good character and the accused goes free. Parishioners are slow to step forward, and the accused may beg the covenant for witnesses.
stages.turned: A magus who swears for the accused is sensed as he takes the oath: the bishop says nothing but marks him. If magic is used to sway witnesses and he notices, he stops the hearing and takes the accused to the cathedral for a full trial, seeing Hell's hand at work.

stages.title: Orris's Dilemma
stages.clues: The court's verdict matters little: what counts is that he smells Hell on a magus. Failing that, he meets one on the road or at an inn, inspects a covenant chapel and feels the aura through any gap in the Aegis, hears a priest's testimony of a spell, or hears a grog's confession.
stages.ignored: He goes home to pray, torn between fighting evil and sparing the weak. Short of knowledge and fearing for his flock in a war, he decides to move slowly: learn about the enemy and strengthen his parishes. The characters probably do not yet know that they have an enemy.

stages.title: A Prudent Populace
stages.clues: Sermons on Prudence, with examples from his court; advice to secular judges; open spiritual counsel. Grogs find less drink, gambling and female company. Locals grow curious, cautious and shrewd at bargaining, give no credit, and the steward sees costs creep up. Vendors rethink trading with wizards, and allies want assurances.
stages.ignored: All Dominion auras in the diocese take a Wise temper. Roll his Holy Influence the first time each season that the characters deal seriously with mundanes there. The bonus goes to Careful, Cautious, Chaste, Practical and Prudent and to sensible choices; the penalty to Ambitious, Overconfident, Naive and Lecherous. Characters and covenfolk feel it only if they live in a Dominion aura.
stages.turned: Perception + Folk Ken: Ease Factor 6 shows something has changed, 9 pinpoints it. Intelligence + Divine Lore 6 traces it to the temper of the Dominion.

stages.title: Gathering Information
stages.clues: A roadside stranger's chat turns oddly probing. An ally asks whether a character ever met the cousin who came asking where he lived. A Quaesitor, told through agents in the papacy that a legate has been asked about the magi, arrives to look into them without saying why, and may seem to be behind it all.
stages.ignored: He questions Archdeacon Geoffrey, who listens for complaints, rumours and ties to notables, so Orris learns their local and ecclesiastic Reputations. Two hired agents work the nearest towns and question friends, serfs and enemies; he warns them off the covenant's servants unless these are known to be unhappy. He writes to the papal legate if the saga has one. He ends with at least most names; at most, each magus's magic, weaknesses and crimes.
stages.stopped: The characters' own agents spot his and turn the tables. Start that story mid-encounter, with the agents fleeing home with news; if they die, no one learns it.

stages.title: The Friars Preacher
stages.clues: Rumours about the magi, and even the covenfolk, come back from the villages. Mundanes turn sullen, hostile or afraid. Grogs turn surly. Tracing the talk leads to Dominicans preaching in a nearby village.
stages.ignored: Brothers Peter, Bartholomew and Alonso preach against the magi by name, and the bad Reputation grows season by season.
stages.stopped: Debate holds the Reputation back; see The Friars Preacher.

stages.title: Blame the Witch
stages.clues: The characters are blamed for every misfortune in the diocese, until they see how many rumours name them and go looking for the source.
stages.ignored: See the side stories: The Bewitched Cows, The Familiar on Trial, The Fallen Church and Unwanted Attention.

stages.title: Invoking St. John
stages.clues: This comes whenever the characters move directly and openly against the bishop or diocese.
stages.ignored: He leads a public ceremony to call down the saint's wrath on them, and repeats it daily if it fails. If the crime was heinous and the saint has not answered, he humiliates the relic the next week to force the saint's hand. If either works, St. John uses Curse of Drowning or Ignis Domini.

stages.title: The Last Sermon
stages.clues: Before a packed congregation, on a great day such as St. John's Mass (December 27), he begs the magi to submit, and commands those he can name to burn their books, break their staves and put aside magic. Most people believe a magus needs his staff (Lords of Men p. 41). A written copy goes to the covenant.
stages.ignored: He waits a week, then acts.
stages.stopped: See the resolutions in this story's secrets.

stages.title: Excommunication
stages.clues: At midnight in the cathedral, with all the clergy he can muster, he excommunicates every wizard his evidence names. All who knowingly keep company with them share the taint.
stages.ignored: Excommunication is a dreadful curse to the God-fearing. Unless the covenfolk and turb are unusually loyal, or the characters take great measures, the covenant empties.
stages.stopped: All effects end when a character is reconciled with the Church. It is meant to heal, not to punish.

stages.title: The Church Knights
stages.clues: The knights enter the city in great pomp, cheered by people who know why they have come. He hopes their name alone will do, but knows he must be ready to shed blood. His resolve is weakening, so he is readier to talk now, though knights guard him by turns.
stages.ignored: They march on the covenant at once.
stages.turned: Spies in the city may give warning.

stages.title: Against the Covenant
stages.clues: The knights fight as veterans of siege warfare.
stages.ignored: They stockade a strong covenant and prepare an escalade, while engineers undermine it. Mass warfare and sieges are in Lords of Men pp. 109-116.

neighbours.secrets:
The bishop suits a covenant with ties to the mundane world; a socially isolated one feels him less. He shows the Order's problem: magi may not meddle with mundanes, but mundanes may meddle with them (p. 50). He can be a new appointment or an incumbent taking a larger part. He will not rest, and every step is meant to drive the magi to submit (p. 62).

The law (p. 55): magic alone is neither a secular nor a canon crime in most of Mythic Europe; its methods or effects may be. Theft or murder by magic is a crime, and idolatry is for the canon court. Bonisagus purged overt idolatry, but theologians and holy magicians still find sacrilege in Hermetic words and gestures (RoP: The Divine Revised Edition pp. 66-69). A witness who hears and understands a casting may roll Intelligence + Artes Liberales to see pagan influences: Ease Factor 9, or 6 for a Ritual. The charge at court is that the magic called on pagan beings, and it rests on hearsay (p. 56). The bishop alone judges, over moral offenses, religious duties and all crimes of clergymen.

Anathema, at the storyguide's choice (p. 62): all Faith Points lost, and none gained while excommunicated without True Faith. One Confidence Point lost on hearing of it. A Local Reputation of Anathema 1. The baptismal name becomes a sympathetic connection. Demons take notice, and a death under it gives Hell the soul. The Gift's penalty takes on the color of impiety. Those with Faith Points sense the danger to their souls. A non-Christian cannot be anathematized and suffers nothing. An excommunicant has no benefit of any sacrament but penance (p. 61).

Ruining his name (pp. 63-64): hard, given a lifetime of good deeds, but possible with time. Magic can forge evidence. Give him a bad Reputation by a significant event and raise it as the friars raise theirs; once it passes his good one it takes precedence. Usually only the pope can remove a bishop (The Church pp. 46-48), and legates test every such petition, so the chapter and the local witnesses must be falsified too. Using local nobles and churchmen invites a charge of meddling.

Submitting (p. 64): he gladly meets magi he thinks repentant. He wants them in humble dress to confess before the congregation, break their staves, swear on the relics never to use magic, give up familiars, surrender their books to the Church and accept penance. Public confession is normal practice. If they do, he undoes all he has done. False oaths risk exposure and Divine anger, such as the Curse of Drowning and anathema. If they refuse, he has no more to say.

The Order's response (pp. 64-65): a magus who dislikes the Church may charge them with endangering their sodales. Those who truly forswear magic may count as having left the Order, losing the Code's protection, and must be slain before they betray the Parma Magica.

Lifting the curse (p. 65; capitulation, hiding or all-out assault being the three main endings). While it lasts he cannot reach terms. A demon's curse ends with the demon, above all if he sees it; the demon or a minion checks on its work now and then, and can be tracked. A hedge or faerie curse likely has a condition to meet, and the one who laid it may want apology or reparation. A Divine curse ends when the characters have learned the lesson, perhaps through public penance. A non-Divine curse could yield to Perdo Vim, but he is hostile and bears relics. Against a Vim specialist, raise the curse's level and draw it from an unfamiliar tradition, so that learning it takes at least another story.

Investigating him (p. 63): monks of his novitiate, penitents who dabbled in magic, people he freed from possession, or the ghost of a witch convicted in his court show that he reacted alike to evil and to magic. A journey to lift the curse could be a pilgrimage (The Church pp. 15-19).

Full disclosure (p. 65): early on he is strong and demands full contrition; later, complicit in excommunication and bloodshed, he wavers. If he suffers The Gift, they cannot persuade him. Those present must have the Gentle Gift, be unGifted, or include him in a Parma Magica. They must convince him magic is not evil by scholarship, mysticism or theology, openly, for he is a good judge of character and deceit would be disastrous, and must correct his ignorance of the Order, which may strain their Oath. Use the debate rules of Houses of Hermes: Societates p. 90, and no dirty tricks.

If he accepts it (p. 65), he still requires confession and penance for known crimes; a church in the covenant, with Sunday Mass for all magi and a Friar Preacher as priest in charge; tithes; care for the diocese's mad and outcast, a possible source of grogs, companions or apprentices; and each magus's confession once a year. He does not demand that they give up magic. He will not bend for a year or so.

Disappearance (pp. 65-66): they leave the diocese, or hide the covenant by powerful magic, with supplies from afar through layers of agents, and go out only in disguise. The bad Reputation fades by 1 experience point a year without suspicion, so it may take decades. Orris will likely be dead by then.

Killing him (p. 66): the Code, the Church's inquiry and possibly a Tribunal conviction follow. The chapter asks the papacy for a successor who knows heresy and the Order, has political weight, and might even be a cardinal, with his own Divine Magic Resistance. Heaven should not leave the murder of a good man unpunished.

neighbours.name: Odd Tales of the Bishop
neighbours.summary: Odd tales of the bishop reach the parishes: sightings that do not fit where he was.

stages.title: A Scoundrel in the Bishop's Likeness
stages.clues: Agents watching the bishop see him slip out of the cathedral one evening in a townsman's clothes. It is Turstan, off to the brothel with his pay from a false blessing arranged by Archdeacon Geoffrey.
stages.ignored: Followed for a few days, he is seen drinking, gambling, keeping loose company and dealing with rogues.
stages.stopped: The real bishop has perfect alibis: Mass before several hundred townsfolk, a guild-master's wedding, alms for the poor.
stages.turned: Denouncing the bishop looks ludicrous and malicious and worsens the characters' Reputations. Unmasking Turstan leads toward the curse.

neighbours.secrets: The book's way to feed the players' guess that Orris must be crooked (p. 63). It is his Story Flaw coming into force during this story.

neighbours.name: Burning Bridges
neighbours.summary: Freemen across the diocese put sense before custom. One town commissions a bridge sooner than walk miles to the old one.
neighbours.secrets: Under the Wise temper (p. 58), the bridge draws a demon builder, such as Architectus (RoP: The Infernal p. 66). The town outwits it three times; shamed, it frames them for diabolism and makes sure the characters see the evidence. If the covenant tries to destroy this "evil" bridge, it only proves the bishop right.

neighbours.name: The Bewitched Cows
neighbours.summary: Cows are bewitched and bread will not rise, and the covenant is blamed.
neighbours.secrets: Blame the Witch (p. 60). The faerie responsible gets no vitality while the characters take the blame, and its cravings change it into something more dangerous. Faeries cannot starve, but defeating it does not end the trouble: the cause of the change must be dealt with. A cognizant faerie might accuse the characters of molestation for stealing its vitality.

neighbours.name: The Familiar on Trial
neighbours.summary: A magus's predatory familiar is accused of eating valuable livestock and is summoned to the manor court for destroying the lord's property.
neighbours.secrets: Blame the Witch (p. 60). Men are sent to the covenant to make sure that the familiar attends.

neighbours.name: The Fallen Church
neighbours.summary: A church in the diocese collapses, and the covenant is blamed.
neighbours.secrets: Blame the Witch (p. 60). The church stood on an ancient vis source. A rival covenant brought it down, trading on the magi's bad Reputation, and claims the vis.

neighbours.name: Unwanted Attention
neighbours.summary: A Quaesitor passing through hears what is being said of the magi and starts asking questions.
neighbours.secrets: Attracting Unwanted Attention (p. 60). If the charges are specific, this may look like a clear case of meddling with mundanes, and he might find enough to bring a case at Tribunal.

neighbours.name: The Quaesitor's Investigation
neighbours.summary: Galerius of House Guernicus is asking questions in the covenant's neighbourhood, and to be investigated by him is known to mean real trouble.

stages.title: A hint of wrongdoing
stages.clues: Some crime or complaint near the covenant reaches him. If the troupe has attended Tribunal, they may have seen him prosecute.
stages.ignored: He comes to the covenant.

stages.title: The interview
stages.clues: He arrives saying plainly what incident he is looking into and asks what they know, who lives there, and who has visited. He calls it an interview, is cordial if brusque, asks hospitality for a night or two, and declines any offer of magical verification as premature, though he remembers it.
stages.ignored: He seems to leave, and stays nearby in disguise to check every answer.

stages.title: Strangers in the villages
stages.clues: Several odd strangers seem to have come to the villages at once, asking about the magi and snooping around places they use. Each wears something grey. A raven is about. Wild rumours spread behind them. Mundanes know a good deal about the magi's visitors and habits, and tell it readily.
stages.ignored: He builds his picture of the magi as deceitful rogues and spreads to anything else suspicious he finds; he can jump from suspicion to suspicion for a long while.
stages.stopped: Grogs and companions, free of the Gift, can shadow him with some comic mistakes, and question the same mundanes. Tracking him by mundane means is lawful, and while they do not know the stranger is a Quaesitor they are probably justified in using magic. Unmasked by magic, he threatens charges and later drops them.

stages.title: Requests for cooperation
stages.clues: If he thinks they are tampering he asks them to stay home for a day or two on some pretext. If confronted he grows angry and hints that they scried on him, though he knows that charge will not stick, and tells them to keep out of his way.
stages.ignored: He files any hindrance as failure to cooperate, on his own testimony.
stages.turned: Solving the real crime while dodging him. Strong evidence against someone else is the one thing that dispels his suspicion; he doubts it, then follows it, and comes to the right answer. He repays this by asking for help with later cases, which earns a good Hermetic Reputation, and may become a prickly friend.

stages.title: Questioning under magic
stages.clues: If they offered, he comes back to hold them to it. Each is taken alone and kept apart, must submit to Sense of the Lingering Magic before and after, and may use no magic. A Quaesitor casts Frosty Breath of the Spoken Lie, held with Maintaining the Demanding Spell and timed by his hourglass. His questions are built to leave no way round, and he ends by asking about any other crime, reported or not.
stages.ignored: Refusal is their right where a question is off the subject, but to him it shows guilt; he threatens, does not prosecute it, and hunts for what they hid.
stages.stopped: The truly innocent can clear themselves in minutes. If he checks their answers and finds nothing he closes the case and files no charges.

stages.title: The private hearing
stages.clues: Summons under the presiding Quaesitor's seal. He arranges to prosecute himself. Before the presiding Quaesitor he offers muck first, then circumstance, then his hard evidence with a triumphant glare. The characters may contest the facts and ask how he came by them; relevance waits for the public hearing.
stages.stopped: If they are innocent he agrees to drop the case rather than be disgraced in public.
stages.turned: The harder they press on his conduct the more agitated he grows, until the presiding Quaesitor turns on him. He may rage, argue and lose, or see what he has done, thunderstruck and in tears. Magi who refuse magical questioning keep the moral high ground.

stages.title: Counter-claim and settlement
stages.clues: A counter-charge of scrying heard now must have been published beforehand; otherwise it waits for the next Tribunal.
stages.ignored: With his credit intact the case goes to public argument, where he has every advantage and presses for harsh penalties. Cooler heads give a minor penalty, a vis fine or a couple of seasons' service, but the magi gain or raise a bad Hermetic Reputation (ArM5 p. 167).
stages.stopped: The presiding Quaesitor presses both sides: charges cut or dropped for counter-claims dropped. Galerius surrenders his letter of authority, goes to Magvillus for several seasons of 'study' and may be moved to another Tribunal. He pays each defendant three pawns of vis a season for their expenses and lost seasons, within a season. He loses Ingrid.

stages.title: The rematch
stages.clues: If he won, he thinks the penalty too light and turns up at any mischief in the region.
stages.ignored: A later Tribunal brings new charges against them, or theirs against him for unlawful investigation. Make it decisive: a final confrontation beats living in dread of one more trial.

neighbours.secrets:
Use him when the magi have done something questionable or have something to hide, or when they are falsely accused by mistake or by design. If there is no reason to suspect them he is no real threat, and can be a short-term ally: do they notice how far he oversteps, and dare they say so? He needs some evidence, however thin, and comes either on a neighbour's complaint or on his own initiative (pp. 67, 69).

What might draw him (pp. 69-70): scrying, which Tribunals punish strictly and which he alone may half excuse; dealing with demons, even unknowingly through tainted vis, for which the penalty is always a March, so give the players clues and a fair chance; deprivation of magical power, over disputed vis, a slain beast near another covenant, or a contested familiar or apprentice, and more than one or two such quarrels brand them habitual troublemakers; mundane interference, which each Tribunal reads differently (Normandy demands proof of ruin to a magus, The Lion and the Lily p. 25, though serving a mundane as a court wizard is always serious); and reckless behaviour, no crime at all, though he thinks it should be. A case with no real merit makes him a paper tiger, a good choice for a troupe new to legal stories, but a conviction can still cost Reputation.

False accusations (p. 70): a disliked wandering magus or redcap vanishes near the covenant, by outlaws, a river or faeries; a neighbour's sanctum is burgled of an invested device or fine book, with the owner's Arcane Connections ended by Perdo Vim, the thief being one of the victim's own covenant; a hedge wizard turned diabolist attacks enemies he shares with the covenant; a magus of another Tribunal secretly sells enchanted items past the usual limits, and the great of the region compete for them. Solving the real crime is the way out. Other sourcebooks' story seeds with accused magi serve too.
